_readme: One table, read by two suites, so the contract and the client mirror are asserted to agree case
by case rather than by inspection. `tests/parity.test.mjs` runs it against src/lib, and
`tests/direct/test_parity.py` runs it against contracts/Holdfast.py.
This exists because of what create_bond does when a rule disagrees. It is payable, and it used to
REVERT rather than refund, and StudioNet does not return gl.message.value on a revert, so a rule
the client got wrong was not a bad error message, it was a stranded stake. A funded transaction
proved that argument insufficient and create_bond is a refusal boundary now: it refunds and
returns the tagged sentence. A wrong rule here costs a signature and a refund at finality instead,
which is cheaper and still worth asserting away.
The two rules below are the two the client cannot avoid reimplementing: the anchor is DERIVED from
the URL and never supplied, so the form has to derive it to show it, and gate D's independence rule
compares normalized forms the promisor never sees.
EVERY NON-ASCII CHARACTER IN THIS FILE IS WRITTEN AS A \u ESCAPE, deliberately. Four of the
normalize cases turn on whether one invisible character is whitespace, and a file carrying those
characters literally cannot be reviewed in a diff or trusted through an editor.
Every `expect` here was computed from the contract's own source, then checked by executing it.
None was typed from reading the TypeScript.
normalize_text: lowercase, collapse whitespace runs to one space, strip everything outside
[a-z0-9 ], trim. In that order, which is the specification and not an implementation detail.
The order has two visible consequences and both are in this table. A stripped character between
two WORDS joins them. A stripped character between two SPACES leaves both spaces behind, because
step 2 has already run and nothing re-collapses them, which is why this function is not
idempotent and why a commitment is hashed exactly once.
The last five cases are the whitespace class itself. Python's \s and JavaScript's \s are
different sets, and the difference changes the OUTPUT rather than just the classification: a
character counted as whitespace collapses to a space and separates its neighbours, and one
counted as ordinary is stripped and JOINS them.

cases.why: the ordinary case
a stripped character between two words joins them
so does a hyphen, which is what makes co-operate and cooperate the same section
a stripped character between two spaces leaves both: two spaces out, not one
the same double space, in a string somebody would really paste
step 4
step 2 over the ASCII whitespace class
a run collapses to one
digits survive step 3
a marker that normalizes to nothing; refused by an earlier check in both languages
the empty string, which the client passes on every keystroke of an empty field
step 3 is ASCII only, so an accent is dropped rather than folded
U+00A0 no-break space is whitespace to both languages
U+2003 em space likewise
U+0085 NEL is whitespace to Python and NOT to JavaScript's \s, so the mirror writes the class out
U+001F unit separator, same story
THE REVERSE. A BOM is whitespace to JavaScript and not to Python, so it JOINS: one word, not two

_readme: Gate B's anchor, derived from the URL's last non-empty path segment: strip the query, drop a
trailing extension of 1 to 5 alphanumeric characters when something is left in front of it,
turn hyphens and underscores into spaces, trim.
`bondable` is whether the normalized anchor reaches MIN_DERIVED_ANCHOR_CHARS. A URL that fails
it cannot be bonded at all, for a reason no form field shows, which is the whole argument for
mirroring this rather than approximating it.

cases.why: the flagship bond's own URL
a trailing slash is not the problem: the walk goes back to the last non-empty segment
a hyphen becomes a space in the anchor, before normalization removes it
underscores too
the query is stripped, so two links to one page derive one anchor
.html goes and .0 stays, because the head before the second dot would be empty
five characters is the longest extension dropped
six is not, so the dot survives into the anchor and then JOINS the two words
a non-alphanumeric extension is not an extension
an empty extension is not dropped, and normalization removes the dot anyway
a leading dot leaves an empty head, so nothing is treated as an extension
the anchor keeps its case; only the comparison is normalized
digits count toward the floor
a bare host derives nothing: bond the page, not the site
and with no trailing slash either
one character is under the floor, so this URL is unbondable
THE TRAP. The extension stripper eats the version, and a version number is exactly what somebody would bond

_readme: Gate D's terminal marker must be independent of gate B's anchor and of every gate C section, in
both directions, by equality or by substring, after normalization.
`overlaps` is null when the spec is usable, "anchor" or "section" when it is not. The contract
checks the anchor first, so no case here collides with both.
The rule exists because two of the four measured pages declared a degenerate marker: one used its
own anchor, the other one of its own sections. On those pages gate D could not fail unless B or C
had already failed, so the composite was three gates wearing four names.

cases.why: the working draft every other lifecycle test is built on
case is normalized away before comparison, so this is the same spec
the measured AWS case: the marker was the anchor, spelled the same
the anchor inside the marker; a sentence somebody would pick from the top of the page
and the other direction: the marker inside the anchor
the measured GCP case: the marker was one of its own sections
a section inside the marker, and no collision with the anchor, so this reaches the section loop
the marker inside a section
the same marker that passes above, refused because a section moved under it
THE ONE INSPECTION MISSES. Two strings that differ raw are equal normalized, so this collides
a three character marker inside a two word derived anchor the promisor never typed
the same marker against a different derived anchor, to show the anchor is what moved

_readme: One measured DIVERGENCE, and the check that makes it unreachable in both languages.
The client's section loop skips an entry that normalizes to empty. The contract's does not: it
asks `terminal in other or other in terminal`, and the empty string is a substring of every
string, so an empty-normalizing section would make EVERY marker overlap. The two would disagree
on every draft carrying such a section.
Neither can be reached, because both languages refuse the section list first: every entry has to
normalize to between MIN_ANCHOR_WORD_CHARS and MAX_ANCHOR_WORD_CHARS. The case below is the
proof of that, asserted rather than assumed, because it is the only thing standing between the
two implementations and a real disagreement.

empty_normalizing_section.why: refused by _require_anchor_words in the contract and by checkAnchorEntries in the client
